newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Confidence strengthens in NZ house mkt-ASB survey.
newsitem.headline: Confidence strengthens in NZ house mkt-ASB survey.

text.p: ASB Bank said on Monday its quarterly Housing Intentions Survey showed a further strengthening in confidence for the housing market in the three months to January 1997, particularly in the Christchurch area.

"Christchurch enjoyed a big leap in confidence, overtaking Wellington and coming out well ahead of Auckland," ASB said, adding that in its last survey, Christchuch respondents had shown the least confidence of the three main centres.
"This major improvement in Christchurch confidence has been driven by reduced concerns about interest rates," ASB Bank economist Rozanna Wozniak said.
"Of those Christchurch participants who said it was a good time to buy, 43 percent cited favourable interest rates, more than double the October figure of 17 percent," she said.
She said the surge in property market confidence was resulting in the reduction of Auckland's lead on house price increases.

"Auckland is no longer the leader in house price inflation. During the nine months to December, house prices in Auckland rose 4.2 percent but in Christchurch they rose 5.1 percent and in Wellington city 7.7 percent," Wozniak said.
"We are definitely seeing the gap in house price inflation between Auckaland and the rest of the country narrow."
She said population growth in Auckland seemed to be starting to slow, which she believed would prevent the regional gap from widening back to the extent of recent years.
"A more stable Auckland housing market bodes well for a more stable interest rate outlook, which is good for economic stability," Wozniak said.
The overall housing market was solid and the short term outlook for interest rates was also positive, she said.
"Recent mortgage rate cuts should be sustained for the first half of the year, in fact further falls in floating mortgage rates are possible.
"However, it would seem likley that mortgage interest rates will start to rise again during the second half of the year."
